los.text: Explain the main examination findings, clinical history, relevant investigations and diagnosis in a patient with obesity (primary and secondary setting)
los.html:
BMI(kg/m²)
  • 25–29.9 overweight
  • 30–34.9 obesity class I; 35–39.9 class II; ≥40 class III.
  • Use thresholds 2.5 lower for South Asian, Chinese, Black African/Caribbean people.
  • Waist-to-height ratio ≥0.5 = central adiposity (health risk).
History
  • Weight trajectory
  • Diet
  • Activity
  • Sleep (OSA: snoring, daytime sleepiness)
  • Mood/binge eating
  • Medications (antipsychotics, steroids, insulin/sulfonylureas, sodium valproate, some antidepressants)
  • Smoking cessation
  • PCOS symptoms
  • Previous attempts
  • Readiness to change
  • Family history.
Examination
  • BMI
  • Waist circumference
  • BP (large cuff)
  • Acanthosis nigricans (insulin resistance)
  • Striae (purple → Cushing's)
  • Hirsutism (PCOS)
  • Goitre/myxoedema (hypothyroid)
  • OA joints
  • Skin intertrigo
  • Signs of HF.
InvestigationsHbA1c/fasting glucose, lipids, LFTs (MASLD/NAFLD; FIB-4), U&E, TFTs; consider overnight dexamethasone suppression (Cushing's), sleep study (OSA), ECG.
Secondary causes(rare)Hypothyroidism, Cushing's, PCOS, hypothalamic damage, genetic syndromes (Prader–Willi, MC4R mutation, leptin deficiency).
Primary careIdentify, measure, brief intervention, tier 2 lifestyle programmes. Secondary/specialist (tier 3–4): complex/severe obesity, drugs (GLP-1 RA), bariatric surgery assessment.
ComplicationsT2DM, hypertension, CVD, OSA, MASLD, OA, GORD, cancers (endometrial, breast, colon), infertility, depression, VTE.

los.text: Describe how appetite regulation affects obesity
los.html:
Hypothalamus = integration centre(arcuate nucleus)
  • Orexigenic (↑ appetite): NPY/AgRP neurons.
  • Anorexigenic (↓ appetite): POMC/CART neurons → α-MSH acts on MC4R (paraventricular nucleus).
Peripheral signals
  • Ghrelin (stomach fundus): ↑ before meals → hunger (the only major orexigenic gut hormone).
  • Leptin (adipocytes, proportional to fat mass): long-term satiety; ↓ NPY, ↑ POMC.
  • Insulin: also signals adiposity to hypothalamus.
  • Satiety hormones: CCK (duodenum), GLP-1 and PYY (L-cells, ileum/colon), vagal stretch.
Hedonic systemMesolimbic dopamine reward (palatable, energy-dense food) can override homeostatic signals.
In obesity
  • Leptin resistance (high leptin, weak effect)
  • After weight loss, ↑ ghrelin and ↓ leptin/PYY/GLP-1 and ↓ energy expenditure → strong drive to regain.
Monogenic obesityMC4R mutation (commonest), leptin or leptin receptor deficiency, POMC deficiency.
Drug relevanceGLP-1 receptor agonists act on these pathways to reduce appetite.

los.text: Describe the principles of treatment and management of severe obesity (pharmaceutical, lifestyle, surgical)
los.html:
Lifestyle (all)
  • Energy deficit (~600 kcal/day), healthy diet
  • ≥150 min/week moderate activity + strength work
  • Behavioural support
  • Target 5–10% weight loss (meaningful health benefits).
  • Tier 2 community programmes
  • Low-energy (800–1200 kcal) or total diet replacement in selected T2DM (remission, e.g. DiRECT trial).
Drugs(with diet/activity)
DrugMechanismNotes
OrlistatPancreatic lipase inhibitor → ↓ fat absorption ~30%Oily stools, faecal urgency, fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption
Semaglutide (Wegovy)GLP-1 receptor agonist: ↓ appetite, slows gastric emptying~15% weight loss. NICE: BMI ≥35 + comorbidity, specialist service, up to 2 years. GI side effects, gallstones, pancreatitis
Tirzepatide (Mounjaro)Dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist~20% weight loss; NICE approved with phased primary care rollout
Liraglutide (Saxenda)Daily GLP-1 RALess effective
  • Bariatric surgery (NICE): BMI ≥40, or 35–40 with significant comorbidity (T2DM, HTN), after tier 3 assessment
    • consider ≥30 with recent-onset T2DM.
    • Sleeve gastrectomy (restrictive + ↓ ghrelin) or Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (restrictive + malabsorptive; best for T2DM remission).
    • Lifelong vitamin/mineral supplements (B12, iron, calcium, vitamin D) and follow-up.
    • Complications: leaks, dumping syndrome, nutritional deficiencies, gallstones.

los.text: Explain primary and secondary hyperlipidaemia, their causes, pathophysiology and management, applying the pharmacology of the drugs and relevant evidence for their benefits to be able to choose and manage effective treatment for individual patients
los.html:
Lipoproteins
  • Chylomicrons (dietary TG), VLDL (hepatic TG) → IDL → LDL (cholesterol to tissues; atherogenic), HDL (reverse cholesterol transport; protective).
  • Lp(a) independent risk factor.
Primary (genetic)
  • Familial hypercholesterolaemia (AD; LDL receptor, ApoB or PCSK9 mutation; ~1 in 250): TC >7.5 mmol/L in adults, tendon xanthomata, premature CVD, corneal arcus <45. Use Simon Broome/Dutch criteria; genetic testing; cascade testing of relatives.
  • Familial combined hyperlipidaemia, familial hypertriglyceridaemia (pancreatitis risk if TG >10).
Secondary
  • T2DM, obesity, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, CKD, cholestasis, alcohol (↑TG), drugs (thiazides, β-blockers, steroids, antipsychotics, retinoids, ciclosporin), pregnancy.
  • Check TSH, HbA1c, LFTs, U&E, urine protein before treating.
Pathophysiology↑ LDL enters intima → oxidised → foam cells → atherosclerosis.
Management (NICE NG238)
  • Lifestyle for all.
  • Primary prevention: QRISK3 ≥10% → atorvastatin 20 mg (CKD: 20 mg).
  • Secondary prevention → atorvastatin 80 mg
  • Aim LDL ≤2.0 mmol/L (or non-HDL ≤2.6).
  • Check lipids at 2–3 months.
DrugMechanismKey points
StatinsInhibit HMG-CoA reductase → ↑ LDL receptorsMyalgia, rarely myopathy/rhabdo (↑ with macrolides, fibrates); check ALT; ~25% relative ↓ in CV events per mmol/L LDL lowered
EzetimibeBlocks NPC1L1 intestinal cholesterol absorptionAdd-on or statin-intolerant
PCSK9 inhibitors (evolocumab), inclisiran (siRNA)↑ LDL receptor recyclingInjections; FH, high-risk secondary prevention
Bempedoic acidATP citrate lyase inhibitorStatin-intolerant
FibratesPPAR-α → ↓ TGSevere hypertriglyceridaemia
Icosapent ethylOmega-3Raised TG on statin, secondary prevention

los.text: Describe how changes in metabolic rate can affect body weight
los.html:
Energy balanceWeight change = energy intake − energy expenditure.
Total energy expenditureBasal/resting metabolic rate (~60–70%) + thermic effect of food (~10%) + physical activity (exercise + NEAT, non-exercise activity thermogenesis; most variable).
BMR depends onLean (fat-free) mass (main determinant), age (↓), sex (men higher), genetics, thyroid hormones, sympathetic tone, temperature, illness (↑ in fever, sepsis, burns).
↓ metabolic rate → weight gainHypothyroidism, ageing (↓ muscle), sedentary lifestyle, drugs (β-blockers), after weight loss (adaptive thermogenesis: expenditure falls more than predicted, promoting regain), smoking cessation.
↑ metabolic rate → weight lossHyperthyroidism, phaeochromocytoma, cancer cachexia (cytokines), COPD (↑ work of breathing), exercise/muscle gain, sympathomimetics.
Brown adipose tissueUCP1 (thermogenin) uncouples oxidative phosphorylation → heat (infants; cold exposure).

los.text: Describe the embryological development of the gastrointestinal tract
los.html:
• Primitive gut forms from endoderm (yolk sac incorporated during folding, week 4).
    • Endoderm → epithelium and glands
    • splanchnic mesoderm → muscle, connective tissue, peritoneum.
RegionDerivativesArteryPain referred to
ForegutOesophagus → 2nd part of duodenum, liver, gallbladder, pancreas, (spleen from mesoderm)Coeliac trunkEpigastrium
Midgut2nd part duodenum → proximal ⅔ transverse colonSMAPeriumbilical
HindgutDistal ⅓ transverse colon → upper anal canalIMASuprapubic
Midgut rotation
  • Physiological umbilical herniation (week 6) → 270° anticlockwise rotation around the SMA → returns to abdomen (week 10).
  • Failure → malrotation (risk of volvulus: bilious vomiting in neonate = emergency), omphalocele (persistent herniation, covered by sac; associated anomalies).
  • Gastroschisis = body wall defect, right of umbilicus, no sac.
Recanalisation failure
  • Duodenal atresia ("double bubble", Down syndrome).
  • Vitelline duct remnant → Meckel's diverticulum (rule of 2s: 2% of people, 2 feet from ileocaecal valve, 2 inches, ectopic gastric/pancreatic tissue → bleeding).
  • Oesophagus–trachea separation failure → tracheo-oesophageal fistula with oesophageal atresia (polyhydramnios, frothy saliva).
  • Hindgut/cloaca: urorectal septum divides it
  • Failure → anorectal malformations.
  • Hirschsprung's: failed neural crest migration → aganglionic distal colon.

los.text: Describe evidence-based behavioural interventions to manage obesity and its related disorders
los.html:
ApproachBrief interventions in primary care (raise the issue sensitively, e.g. "Let's Talk" / very brief advice) → referral to multicomponent programmes (diet + activity + behaviour change).
Models
  • Transtheoretical (Stages of Change): precontemplation → contemplation → preparation → action → maintenance (± relapse)
  • Tailor advice to stage.
  • COM-B model: Capability, Opportunity, Motivation → Behaviour.
  • Health Belief Model, Theory of Planned Behaviour.
Effective behaviour change techniques
  • Goal setting (SMART)
  • Self-monitoring (food diary, weighing, step counts)
  • Feedback
  • Problem-solving
  • Action planning
  • Stimulus control (remove cues)
  • Social support
  • Relapse prevention planning
  • Rewards.
Motivational interviewingCollaborative, evokes the patient's own reasons for change; OARS (Open questions, Affirmations, Reflections, Summaries); roll with resistance.
CBT-based approaches for emotional eating/binge eating.
Evidence
  • Multicomponent programmes give modest (~3–5 kg) losses
  • Maintenance support improves long-term outcome.
  • Weight stigma worsens outcomes, so use person-first, non-judgemental language.
Population/environmentSugar levy, food labelling, planning around fast-food outlets, active travel.
